title: Object Detection in Degraded UAV RGB Imagery: A Scoping Review of Robustness Evaluation
content: Object detection from unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) must often operate on images degraded by blur, noise, low illumination, haze, adverse weather, compression and transmission damage, and the severity of these effects depends on flight altitude, ground sampling distance (GSD) and atmospheric path length. Published robustness claims are nevertheless rarely comparable. This scoping review, reported according to PRISMA-ScR, counts studies as the unit of inclusion and interprets each robustness claim through the within-study comparison that supports it. We relate degradation mechanisms to acquisition geometry and detection failures, organize mitigation methods by the information they consume during training and the computation they retain at inference, and code the 176 included studies (from 4913 screened records) by degradation family, provenance and training access. Evidence is concentrated on haze (75 studies) and low light (74). Natural-capture evidence is absent for noise and scarce for compression and transmission damage, and only 9 of 45 natural night-time studies report a same-model daytime reference. Our re-analysis of published results identifies recurring pitfalls: gains on corrupted images with unchanged relative retention, dehazing gains on synthetic haze that reverse on natural haze, and real-domain tests that include labeled target fine-tuning. We propose six evaluation designs (P0–P5), which a single study may combine, and a minimum reporting checklist that includes altitude and GSD, so that future robustness claims can be compared.
